title: Write the lexer

prereqs.why: This is the scanning stage itself — the first point at which flat text acquires any structure.
Knowing which stage this is tells you what the lexer is allowed to care about and what it must leave to the parser.

statement:
Read **one line** containing an arithmetic expression and print its tokens, one per line.

The language has exactly five kinds of token:

| Kind | What it is | Printed as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| number | one or more digits | `NUM 42` |
| identifier | a letter or `_`, then letters, digits or `_` | `IDENT total_2` |
| parenthesis | `(` or `)` | `LPAREN (` or `RPAREN )` |
| operator | any other non-space character | `OP +` |

Spaces and tabs separate tokens and are otherwise ignored. An operator is always a single character — there are no two-character operators in this language.

### Example

```
input:   x1 + 42 * (y - 3)

output:  IDENT x1
         OP +
         NUM 42
         OP *
         LPAREN (
         IDENT y
         OP -
         NUM 3
         RPAREN )
```

Note that whitespace is *not* required between tokens: `1+2` is three tokens, and so is `1 + 2`. That is the whole reason a lexer has to look at characters rather than just splitting on spaces.
hints: Splitting the line on spaces will pass the first sample and fail everything else. `1+2` has no spaces in it and is still three tokens.
Walk the string with an index. At each position, decide what kind of token starts here from the first character, then consume as many characters as belong to it.
Numbers and identifiers are the only tokens longer than one character, and each is a run of characters of a particular class. Everything else advances the index by exactly one.

cases.expect:
IDENT x1
OP +
NUM 42
OP *
LPAREN (
IDENT y
OP -
NUM 3
RPAREN )
